item.title: AVS in Canton Uri: clearing house guide
item.description: How the first pillar works in Canton Uri: compensation fund, calculation of the AVS annuity and supplementary benefits for those who do not reach the minimum living wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The first Swiss pillar (AVS/AHV) is managed by cantonal and professional clearing houses - Supplementary benefits (PC) cover the difference when the AVS income is not sufficient at the minimum living - The Canton Uri Compensation Fund is the cantonal institution of reference for registrations and annuities - CPs are calculated on the basis of the recognised expenses and the applicant's computable income
## Key facts - **What**: Management of the first AVS pillar and complementary services (PC) in Canton Uri - Where: Canton Uri, central Switzerland - Who: Uri Cantonal Compensation Fund (Ausgleichskasse Uri) - When: System in force on a federal basis, with cantonal application - How: Contribution payments, calculation of income according to federal scales, PC application at the cantonal fund - Regulatory reference: federally regulated AVS (LAVS), PC according to the LPC
In the Swiss three-column system, the first pillar — Old Age and Survivors Insurance (AVS/AHV) — is the basis of compulsory social security for those residing or working in Switzerland. Each canton has its own cantonal compensation fund that acts as an operational counter for workers, employers, pension recipients and claimants of supplementary benefits. In the canton of Uri, the cantonal compensation fund is the entity designated to receive wage declarations, collect AVS/AI/IPG contributions and manage applications for ## How supplementary benefits work in the Canton of Uri
Supplementary benefits (SB) to OASI/DI are regulated at the federal level by the Supplementary Benefits Act (LPC), but their payment and operational management is entrusted to the cantons. In Uri, responsibility lies with the cantonal compensation fund in collaboration with the social services, which process the application, collect the documents and calculate the monthly amount due.
### The calculation formula
The SB amount is given by the difference between recognised expenses and computable income. Recognised expenses include the amount for basic needs (distinguished for single persons, couples, families), the actual rent (up to a recognised maximum), medical and paramedical expenses not covered by other insurances, and other items provided for by the LPC. Computable income, on the other hand, consists of the OASI/DI pension, any income from work, income from assets (assets above an exemption threshold are converted into notional income), third-party benefits and family allowances. If the difference is positive, the applicant is entitled to SB for the corresponding amount.
### Who is entitled to SB
Persons who receive an OASI or DI pension, or who — within a certain time horizon — would be entitled to a pension, are entitled to SB, provided their economic situation meets the legal criteria. The application may also be submitted by persons who have not yet reached the reference age, if they receive a DI pension. For recipients of modest pensions, SB is often the difference between a poor old age and a dignified old age: in many situations the OASI pension alone does not even cover the rent and basic expenses.
### Hypothetical scenario: a couple with a minimum pension
Consider a couple residing in Uri in which both have paid full contributions but with always low-to-medium incomes, receiving two reduced OASI pensions and living in a rented apartment. If the recognised expenses (basic needs for a couple, actual rent, health insurance premiums) exceed the sum of the OASI pensions and other income, the difference is covered by the SB, paid monthly by the compensation fund. The same person, with a small additional income from a reduced gainful activity, would see the SB amount reduced but not necessarily the entitlement cancelled.
### Implications for the family budget
Obtaining SB means for many elderly people being able to stay in their own home, pay health insurance premiums (LAMal) and maintain a minimum standard of living. The SB is recalculated annually, and the beneficiary is required to communicate any change in income, assets or housing situation. In Uri, as in the rest of Switzerland, SB applications are growing structurally, linked both to the increase in housing costs and to the share of reduced pensions for careers with low incomes or contribution interruptions.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Practical procedure: how to submit your application in Uri
Obtaining the AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance) pension and, if necessary, supplementary benefits (PC) in the Canton of Uri requires a few precise steps. The procedure is defined at the federal level, but the point of contact is the cantonal compensation office of Uri (Ausgleichskasse Uri).
### Step 1 — Check your contribution record
Before submitting any application, it is useful to request an extract of the individual account (CI) from the FSIO (UFAS/BSV) or through the compensation office. The individual account lists all contributions paid, recorded income, and any gaps. If missing years appear, discuss with the compensation office the possibility of a retroactive payment.
### Step 2 — Applying for the AVS pension
The AVS pension is not paid automatically: it must be requested from the Uri compensation office, usually a few months before reaching the reference age. The office sends the forms, collects the required documents (family record, salary certificates, any periods of work abroad) and forwards the file for calculation. The first pension is normally paid retroactively from the month of application, not earlier.
### Step 3 — Possible application for supplementary benefits (PC)
If the AVS pension — alone or together with other income — does not cover the vital minimum needs, the PC phase opens. The application is submitted to the Uri compensation office with the following typical documents: AVS/AI pension decision, rent certificate and lease agreement, bank and securities statements, insurance policies (life, 3a), and spouse's income certificates. The office checks the recognised expenses and computable income and issues the decision.
### Step 4 — Reporting changes
Every relevant change — rent change, inheritance, sale of property, start of a gainful activity, death of a spouse — must be reported to the compensation office within the set deadlines. Failure to report may lead to a reduction or revocation of the PC, with recovery of amounts already paid.
### Timelines and deadlines
Decision times vary depending on the complexity of the case: a simple AVS application can be processed in a few months, while a PC file with complex documentation may take longer. It is advisable to submit the PC application immediately after the pension starts, to avoid income gaps. Specific deadlines apply to applications for retroactive payment of missing contributions, to be checked case by case with the compensation office.
### Where to get information
For any information on AVS and PC in the Canton of Uri, the first point of contact is the cantonal compensation office of Uri (Ausgleichskasse Uri). The canton's official website provides the address, opening hours and downloadable forms.

item.title: School in Ticino: VPOD asks for staff, time and resources
item.description: At the opening of the schools, the VPOD Ticino teachers' committee led by Matteo Finali relaunches the request to invest in the working conditions of school staff.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Start of the school year: classrooms and teachers return to work - VPOD Ticino: we need staff, time and resources for the school - Inclusion cannot rest only on the goodwill of teachers - Quality of the offer must not depend on the Municipality of residence
## Key facts - **What**: Appeal by the VPOD Ticino teachers' committee to invest in the working conditions of school staff at the start of the new year - When: Start of the new school year (specific date not indicated in the source) - Where: Ticino, with reference to the Municipal Schools of Massagno and Bellinzona (Piazza Grande area) - Who: Matteo Finali, co-chair of the VPOD Ticino teaching committee and professor of Music Education - Trade union subject: VPOD (union that collectively organizes the staff of the school in Ticino) - Focus: Adequate staff, coordination times, equipped services, work-life balance - Key word evoked: "time" as a resource to be brought back to the center of the debate
With the opening of schools for the new school year, Matteo Finali — co-chair of the VPOD Ticino teachers' committee and teacher of Music Education at the Municipal Schools of Massagno and Bellinzona (Piazza Grande area) — relaunches a public reflection on the working conditions of those who teach. The article, signed as a contribution of opinion, starts from a simple observation: school is not only the transmission of knowledge, but also a relationship, listening, motivation and Finali's speech does not introduce figures or specific measures: it is a contribution of opinion that sets a framework of priorities. However, the keywords used — organic, time, inclusion, working conditions — touch levers that have a direct reflection on the organization of public school in Ticino, and by extension on the lives of families that entrust their children to the cantonal school system.
### What does "time" mean in the Ticino school
The reference to "time" as a resource to be protected is the analytical heart of the text. Finali lists a series of activities that have multiplied around teaching: meetings, documentation, coordination, interviews, training, administrative tasks. The point is not to judge these activities — some are mandatory, others required by school regulations — but to recognize that they subtract hours from classroom activity. For a teacher, this means less preparation for lessons, less availability for individual difficulties, less room for the educational relationship. For families, it means more pressured teachers and, potentially, a less personalised training offer.
### Inclusion and staff

VPOD is presented as the body that collectively organises school staff. ### What teachers can do
Finali explicitly mentions the risk that the time devoted to the relationship with students may be compressed. The union response proposed is to bring 'time' back to the centre of the debate. The article points out that the quality of the school offer should not depend on the municipality. For parents, the very issue is this: the educational offer can vary at a local level. ### The word 'time' as a compass
The word that Finali invites us to put back at the centre is 'time'. Time to prepare lessons, time to coordinate with colleagues, time to follow each student. It is a demand for method before anything else: asking that the organisation of the school return to serving teaching and the educational relationship, rather than the other way around.

item.title: Graubünden: no new fines for detour traffic
item.description: The Grand Council of Grisons rejects the UDC motion by 67 votes to 41: no anti-divert project until a ruling on the Birsfelden model.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The Grand Council of Grison has decided to suspend consideration of new diversion anti-trafficking measures - The Executive awaits the ruling on the Birsfelden (BL) model, where a transit ban with automated fines has been in force since 2025 - The UDC motion was rejected by 67 votes to 41
## Key facts - **What**: The Grand Council of Graubünden has decided to wait for the judicial ruling on the Birsfelden model before evaluating new sanctions against diversionary traffic - When: The decision was made today; in Birsfelden the ban has been in place since 2025 - Where: Graubünden, on the north-south axis and on the N28; the reference model is located in Birsfelden (BL) - Who: The Grand Council of Grison, the Government of Grison, the UDC of Grison - Amount: Fines in Birsfelden are triggered for those who stop less than 15 minutes in the affected areas
The Grand Council of Graubünden decided today to align itself with the government's position on diversionary traffic during periods of congestion. The Executive has chosen not to adopt further measures before having a final judgment on the model of sanctions adopted by the municipality of Birsfelden, in the canton of Basel-Country.
On the north-south axis and on the N28 in the Graubünden, queues regularly form during the high tourist season and on weekends. Many motorists deviate on the roads of the surrounding countries, to the point that even the residents struggle to transit.
The Grison CDU had ### The implications for Graubünden residents
The decision of the Greater Grison Council temporarily leaves the situation unchanged for those living in the areas affected by diversion traffic. Residents of the north-south axis and the N28 will continue to face traffic jams during the peak tourist season and on weekends, with motorists inevitably diverting onto secondary municipal roads.
The Birsfelden model, which the UDC in Grison was inspired by, provides for automated penalties for those who transit in areas subject to prohibition without stopping for at least 15 minutes. It is an approach that aims to discourage the use of neighbourhood streets as shortcuts during queuing periods, but its applicability in a canton with a strong tourist vocation such as Graubünden remains to be verified.
### The tourist node raised by the PLR
PLR deputy Bruno Loi highlighted an aspect that goes beyond mere traffic management. "We must not forget that Birsfelden's solution would hit and sanction guests in the first place," he noted, recalling that Graubünden lives on tourism. This argument has been heard in a parliament where the economic component linked to the tourism sector has a considerable specific weight.
Center deputy Franz Sepp Caluori summed up the majority's approach: "Let's calmly look for a smart solution." A position that prioritizes caution over adoption

To understand what awaits Graubünden, it is worth examining the mechanism already in operation in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. In Birsfelden, since 2025, several residential streets have been closed to through traffic during congestion periods. Passage control is carried out in an automated manner: cameras or other devices detect vehicles crossing the restricted zones.
A fine is issued to those who pass through without stopping for at least 15 minutes in the affected areas. The aim is to distinguish between those who live in or need to access services in the area and those who simply use it as a shortcut to avoid queues on the main route.
### The automated control procedure
The system adopted in Birsfelden is based on detection technologies that make it possible to identify vehicles in transit and verify the duration of the stop. If the restriction is not respected, the vehicle owner receives a fine. The procedure is similar to that used for other automatically detected violations, such as speeding or running red lights.
### Next steps
Graubünden currently has no defined timeline for the ruling on the Birsfelden model. The cantonal government has committed to monitoring the judicial situation and to evaluating any measures only once there is full legal clarity. In the meantime, the municipalities affected by diversion traffic can continue to use the traffic management tools already available, such as prohibition signs or temporary one-way systems.
For those who live in or regularly travel through the affected areas, the only certainty for the moment is that the situation will remain unchanged at least until there are significant developments on the judicial or political front.

item.title: UBS issues first 2 billion yuan Panda bond
item.description: UBS lands on the Chinese bond market by raising 2 billion yuan with a five-year Panda bond at a fixed rate of 1.78%.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - UBS issues its first Panda bond for 2 billion yuan. - The transaction marks a first for the Swiss banking sector. - The five-year issue rate is set at 1.78%.
## Key facts - **What**: Issue of the first five-year Panda bond - Who: UBS led by Sergio Ermotti - Amount: 2 billion yuan (240 million francs) - Rate: Fixed coupon at 1.78% - Context: Corporate expansion and local financing
UBS enters the Chinese bond market with a historic issue: a billion yuan loan, the first for a Swiss bank, which marks a turning point in the financial integration between Switzerland and the world's second largest economy. As reported by the ATS agency, the Swiss banking giant has placed a so-called 'Panda bond' at five years, collecting about 2 billion yuan, equal to a value of about 240 million francs.
### A breakthrough for Swiss finance
The operation on the capital market of the People's Republic represents an absolute novelty for the Swiss [istituti bancari](nav:banks). A Panda bond and a renminbi-denominated bond issued by a non-Chinese entity and placed directly among investors in mainland China. Industry experts consider this placement a move of strategic importance, made in a phase of progressive fragmentation of international trade and markets.
The institute led by Sergio Ermotti thus aligns itself with the ### Corporate Integration and Diversified Markets
The bond placement crowns a path of operational growth that is already well established in the Chinese market. The bank closed 2025 with local revenue growing by more than 40%, simultaneously recording a pre-tax profit that more than doubled. On the corporate front, last April the institution took full control of UBS Securities, a brokerage firm based in the Asian country, raising its equity stake from 67% to 100%.
According to the analysis by John Plassard, partner at Cité Gestion—a private bank also present in Lugano—this step confirms that Beijing's bond sector is becoming a credible alternative to traditional markets denominated in dollars and euros. The presence of more transparent regulations and the availability of longer maturities make the Chinese domestic market particularly competitive for fundraising.
### Direct Access to Local Currency
Having multiple funding channels provides a tangible advantage to avoid exclusive dependence on US or European investors. Issuing yuan-denominated bonds on the domestic circuit consolidates the institution's standing with regulatory authorities and local investors, strengthening both wealth management activities and domestic lending capabilities. Raising funds in the local currency directly supports on-the-ground operations, reducing exposure to fluctuations monitored also through [currency exchange](nav:exchange) tools and positioning the bank right alongside the wave of new listings in the tech and artificial intelligence sectors. ### Strategic positioning and liquidity management
The choice to issue debt directly in the People's Republic has greater operational advantages than a traditional offshore issuance conducted on the Hong Kong market. The structure of the loan allows resources to be found on particularly favourable terms, exploiting a rate of 1.78% made possible by the considerable availability of liquidity among Chinese savers and institutional investors.
This type of transaction reflects the global dynamics that influence the stability of the Swiss economic system, whose capital strength is closely monitored by bodies such as the SNB/SNB in the context of the evolution of the financial market. For operators and professionals active in Switzerland, access to diversified international financing channels contributes to strengthening the global competitiveness of the main employers in the Swiss tertiary sector.
### Tools and perspectives for professionals in Switzerland
The growth of international activities and the diversification of funding sources consolidate the solidity of the large Swiss banking groups, with indirect effects on the employment market and internal salary levels. item.title: Graubünden: guaranteed cash payment for services
item.description: The Grand Council approves the Bettinaglio counter-project: taxes and transport in Graubünden can be paid in cash, despite digitalisation.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Guaranteed cash payment for taxes and public services in Graubünden. - The Bettinaglio counter-project approved with 83 votes in favor. - The popular initiative has already collected over 16,000 signatures in the Canton. - Exceptions provided for security reasons or technical impossibility.
## Key facts - **What**: Parliamentary resolution for the use of cash in public services - When: Grand Council decision of November 13, 2024 - Where: Canton of Graubünden (Chur) - Who: Graubünden Grand Council, SVP, Martin Bettinaglio (The Centre) - Amount: 16,000 signatures collected (4,000 quorum required)
The Grand Council of Graubünden has established a principle that directly affects the daily lives of residents and taxpayers: the possibility of paying in cash for cantonal and municipal taxes, as well as for the use of public infrastructure, must be guaranteed. The decision, reached today in the chamber, represents a regulatory anticipation of what is requested by a popular initiative currently following its path towards a vote. The parliamentary debate concluded with a clear majority in favor of the counter-project presented by Grand Councilor Martin Bettinaglio, a representative of The Centre, which received 83 votes in favor, compared to 30 against and four abstentions.
### Political genesis and the compromise in the chamber The issue was initially raised by a motion from the SVP, which called for strong protections for the use of physical money in dealings with the public administration. The original text was however softened through Bettinaglio's counter-project, which sought a balance between the citizen's freedom of choice and the operational needs of the offices. Even the SVP itself agreed to mitigate its initial demands in order to see the core principle approved in the cantonal legislature. However, some gray areas remain, as pointed out by the FDP, which voted against the proposal. The Liberals highlighted a potential overlap with the popular initiative of the same name, which, proceeding in parallel, risks creating a dual regulatory track. Furthermore, the 'reasonableness' clause was criticized, deemed too vague to precisely define when a public body can legitimately refuse banknotes. This decision will influence how citizens interact with [public transport](nav:transport) and municipal counters, reinforcing the role of cash in an era of push towards the digitalization of payments. ### The popular initiative and the case of direct sales The political ferment surrounding physical money in Grisons did not emerge in a vacuum, but is the result of a significant popular mobilization called 'Cash payment of public services', also defined by its promoters as the 'Initiative against discrimination'. The committee, led by retiree Berta Caminada, gave voice to a widespread discontent resulting from operational decisions made by entities such as PostBus and the Department of Infrastructure, Energy and Mobility. The spark was the abolition of direct cash ticket sales by onboard staff on buses, a measure that prompted Caminada to first launch a petition, which gathered 8,000 signatures, and then the initiative itself.
The numbers from the signature collection, cited during the debate by the president of the SVP parliamentary group Stefan Metzger, describe massive support: since June, over 16,000 signatures have been filed, a figure four times higher than the 4,000 required to bring the issue to a popular vote. The orientation of the initiative is very similar to that of the counter-project just approved by Parliament, calling for cash to remain a valid means of payment for taxes, public parking, and even access to public toilets. It is essential to note that the obligation to accept would not be extended to private sector companies, limiting the scope of action only to public or state-co-financed companies. This aspect is crucial for those who must evaluate their [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) and daily expense management methods in the Canton, as it guarantees a plurality of options for mandatory payments to the public entity.
### Exceptions to the cash rule Despite the general principle being established, the resolution provides for specific safeguard clauses. Cash payment may be limited or excluded if the offer is not reasonable or appropriate for prevailing reasons. These include the safety of operators, protection against possible abuse, and technical impossibility. This last point particularly concerns automated systems that are not designed to handle coins or banknotes and whose adaptation would involve disproportionate costs. The debate now shifts to the practical application of these concepts: what is meant by 'reasonable' remains the most debated point, with the risk that the discretion of individual offices could limit the effectiveness of the new rule.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Procedures and impact for residents For citizens residing in Grisons, the Grand Council's resolution opens a transitional phase in the management of financial relations with the State. Once implemented, the legislation will allow visiting municipal or cantonal counters to pay taxes without necessarily having credit cards or banking applications. The procedure for paying taxes, which usually occurs via payment slips, must therefore maintain channels that allow the use of cash, facilitating segments of the population less accustomed to technology or those who prefer not to digitally track every transaction. Also for the use of infrastructure, such as public parking, municipalities will have to evaluate whether current systems respect the criterion of reasonableness in accepting physical money.
The next steps include: - Integration of the cash principle into cantonal and municipal legal bases. - Technical evaluation of ticket vending machines for [public transport](nav:transport) and parking meters. - Possible popular vote on the initiative, should the promoters decide not to withdraw it despite the approval of the counter-project.
Those living or working in the Canton must consider that, although the public sector is moving towards this protection of cash, private transactions remain regulated by contractual freedom. Therefore, for expenses related to rent or purchases at commercial establishments, payment methods will continue to be established by individual providers. To correctly plan your family budget in Switzerland, it is useful to consult updated tools on fixed expenses and taxes. If you want to learn more about how these decisions influence your purchasing power, you can use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to get a clear overview of deductions and net income management. For those considering settling in the region, it is advisable to consult the guides on [living in Switzerland](nav:living-ch) to better understand the dynamics between public payments and the management of local bureaucracy.

item.title: Energy rehabilitation, new financing model
item.description: The Confederation and the Cantons are launching a new joint model to boost the energy efficiency of Swiss buildings. Consultation in the autumn.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Energy renovation of buildings encouraged by the new model. - Objective: to reduce consumption and CO2 emissions. - Public consultation in the autumn.
## Key facts - **What**: New joint financing model for building energy renovation. - When: Consultation in the autumn, revision of the energy ordinance. - Where: Switzerland (Confederation and Cantons). - Who: Cantonal Energy Directors' Conference (EnDK) and Federal Office of Energy. - Objective: Improve energy efficiency, reduce consumption and emissions, protect from heat.
Switzerland is preparing for an acceleration in the field of building energy rehabilitation. A new joint financing model, the result of collaboration between the Confederation and the Cantons, aims to encourage interventions aimed at improving the energy efficiency of Swiss real estate. The primary objective is twofold: on the one hand, to reduce energy consumption and, consequently, CO2 emissions; on the other, to improve the protection of buildings from increasing climatic stresses, as demonstrated by the recent persistent heat waves. This new instrument is part of the broader framework of the Buildings Programme, which will undergo a reorganisation from 2028. ## Key facts - **What**: Slight drop in the price of electricity for domestic utilities and introduction of seasonal tariffs - When: News will start from 2027; today's communication from Repower - Where: Network area of the Repower group, mainly in Graubünden - Who: Repower, an energy group based in Poschiavo (GR) - Amount: CHF 1,449 per year for a family of 4 with consumption of 4,500 kWh (-20 CHF, -1.4%) - New: Grischunpower product with more expensive rates in winter and cheaper in summer, average annual energy price unchanged - New product: Optima, hourly variable rate with three levels (green/yellow/red) - Network investments: CHF 30-40 million per year for upgrades and smart grids
Repower, the energy group based in Poschiavo, will slightly reduce electricity prices for domestic utilities in its network area in Graubünden. The announcement came today from the company: in 2027 a family of four with an annual consumption of 4,500 kilowatt hours will pay 1,449 francs of electricity, twenty francs less than the current year. The percentage change is -1.4%.
The ## What's changing for families in Graubünden The reduction of twenty francs per year on a standard consumption of 4,500 kWh is contained — equal to 1.4% — but comes at a time when the cost of living and energy bills remain a sensitive item in the domestic budget throughout Switzerland. For a typical household, the savings amount to about 1.67 francs per month, a figure that alone does not change the structure of spending, but adds to other signs of moderation in energy prices.
It is important to underline a technical detail: the savings indicated refer to Repower's standard Grischunpower supply and do not include municipal taxes. In Graubünden — as in the rest of Switzerland — the final electricity bill consists of the sum of energy, network use, taxes and VAT. The increase in real consumption, a change of category (for example, a change to the Optima tariff) or an increase decided by the individual municipalities can easily cancel or exceed the twenty francs of savings indicated.
### Seasonal Differentiation: Opportunity and Attention The logic of the differentiated tariff is well known: shifting consumption in the summer months, when hydroelectric and solar production is more abundant, is in the best interest of both the customer and the grid. Repower explains this by recalling the greater availability of renewable energy in the summer and the trend of the electricity markets.
For a Grisonese family, the practical question becomes: when is it best to move loads?

item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in Canton Uri
item.description: How to find an internship in Canton Uri: contract, salary, professional maturity and concrete steps to apply.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - In Switzerland, vocational training is regulated at the federal level by the LFPr - The Canton of Uri manages the network of traineeship posts through the cantonal office of vocational training - Apprenticeship normally takes place in 3 or 4 years, depending on the profession - Federal professional maturity is compatible with the internship and opens the doors to sup
## Key facts - **What**: dual vocational training (company + vocational school + intercompany courses) - When: 3- or 4-year internship, with the possibility of parallel professional maturity - Where: Canton Uri, cantonal vocational training authority - Who: UST/BFS for federal statistics, State Secretariat for Training (SEFRI) for legal bases - Amount: the apprentice's salary is set by the employer according to the sector and the year of internship (cantonal reference rates, annual amount to be verified year by year)
Vocational training in Switzerland is based on a federal legal basis, the Vocational Training Act (LFPr), and is divided into three places of learning: the training company, the vocational school and intercompany courses. In the Uri Canton, as in the rest of the Confederation, this dual model allows those who finish compulsory school to choose a qualified professional path directly, without necessarily going through high school. The watchword is permeability: after a federal certificate ## # Finding an internship: concrete channels The search for an internship position in Canton Uri passes through some standard channels. The first is the Cantonal Vocational Training Office, which publishes the list of available traineeships every year and accompanies young people in their choice. The second is the national platform Orientamento.ch, which gathers offers from all Swiss training companies. The third is direct contact with companies, often the most effective in smaller cantons such as URIs, where the economic fabric is made up of many SMEs.
A good practice is to start the research one year before the start of the internship. Training companies select candidates in the spring for the beginning of the following summer, although deadlines vary from industry to industry. For the craft and technical sectors — particularly present in a mountain canton such as Uri — spontaneous applications are often well received, especially if accompanied by an updated curriculum vitae and a personalised letter of motivation.
### Internship contract: what it must contain The traineeship contract is governed by the Code of Obligations (CO) and the Vocational Training Ordinance (OFPr). It must indicate the duration, the monthly or annual salary of the apprentice, the weekly working hours, the days of vacation (minimum 4 weeks, 5 weeks for those under 20), the person responsible for training in
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete application procedure: step by step For those who want to start an apprenticeship in Canton Uri, the realistic path unfolds in six steps.
1. Self-assessment and choice of profession. Consult the official list of available professions at the Cantonal Office of Vocational Education and the guidance tools at orientamento.ch. It is also useful to do a trial internship at a company to test the chosen profession.
2. Active search for an apprenticeship position. Send written applications to companies in the sector, register on the cantonal platform for apprenticeship positions, and contact directly the guidance office of the secondary school.
**3. Presentation interview.** Present yourself with a portfolio of school assessments, internship certificates, and personal references. Small Uri-based companies often also assess personal motivation and knowledge of the local area.
4. Signing of the apprenticeship contract. Check that the contract specifies: profession, duration, salary, weekly working hours, holidays, vocational school, and the contact person at the company. Keep a copy signed by both parties.
5. Registration at the vocational school. The company normally forwards the data to the school, but the apprentice (or whoever holds parental authority, if a minor) must confirm the registration.
6. Registration with social insurance. The company registers the apprentice with the mandatory insurances: AVS/AHV, accident insurance (LAINF/LAA), AD/AC, and pension fund if the coordinated salary exceeds the LPP/BVG threshold. In Canton Uri as in the rest of Switzerland, anyone who changes canton or begins a gainful activity must also take out mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) within three months.
### Mistakes to avoid Underestimating the time needed for the search is the most frequent mistake: many companies close selections in spring. Not carefully reading the federal ordinance for the chosen profession leads to discovering exam subjects or admission conditions too late. Finally, not considering the vocational baccalaureate at the time of signing the contract can later force more complicated schooling choices.

item.title: Energy transition, Switzerland is fifth in Europe but wind remains weak
item.description: Study SES 2025: 4872 kWh per capita from renewables, solar at 878 kWh. Wind stopped at 18 kWh, 25th place out of 28 countries.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Switzerland fifth in the EU for renewables per capita: 4872 kWh - Solar: new record at 878 kWh per capita, tenth place - Wind: only 18 kWh per capita, 25th place out of 28 countries - 70.8% of the electricity consumed in Switzerland is renewable
## Key facts - **What**: annual ranking of renewable energy production per capita - When: 2025 data, published today (study dated yesterday) - Where: comparison between Switzerland and 27 EU Member States - Who: Schweizerische Energie-Stiftung (SES), Swiss Energy Foundation - Study title: Dekarbonisierung der schweizer Energieversorgung im Europäischen Vergleich - Per capita solar amount CH: 878 kWh (historical record) - Wind energy per capita CH: 18 kWh - Renewable share of electricity consumption CH: 70.8%
The Swiss energy transition runs, but at two speeds. The Schweizerische Energie-Stiftung (SES) puts it in black and white in the annual study "Dekarbonisierung der schweizer Energieversorgung im Europäischen Vergleich", which for 2025 compares the Confederation with the 27 countries of the European Union. The verdict is positive overall, with the fifth place for electricity production from renewable sources per capita: 4,872 kilowatt-hours (kWh), behind Sweden (11,478 kWh), Finland (8,245), Austria (6,655) and Denmark (5,066).
The Swiss figure, SES explains, is mainly based on hydroelectric power, which alone generates more than half of the current produced in Switzerland. If you report the ## Analysis: what it means for bills and the Swiss energy mix
The picture that emerges from the SES study is a half-full glass, with an obvious crack on the wind side. The Confederation can boast a continental record in the share of renewables in electricity consumption: 70.8%, of which almost 55 percentage points come from hydropower and around 13 from solar power. A figure that earns it fifth place in Europe, behind Sweden (92%), Austria (88%), Denmark (82%) and Portugal (71%). In practical terms, seven kWh out of every ten consumed in Switzerland come from sun, water or wind.
### Electrification still low
There is, however, another indicator that tempers the enthusiasm: the overall degree of electrification of the energy system. Electricity accounts for 26.7% of total energy consumption in Switzerland, seventh in the SES ranking. The record goes to Sweden, which still stops at 35.3%: a sign that most of the energy consumed in Europe still depends on other sources, not necessarily green. For the Confederation, therefore, the challenge is twofold: producing more clean electricity and, at the same time, shifting to electricity those segments currently dominated by fossil fuels, such as heating and transport.
### Where Switzerland can still grow
The study stresses that the Confederation has a not insignificant expansion potential. Per capita figures in several more northerly countries, where solar irradiation is objectively lower, remain higher. In other words: with fewer hours of sunlight, more solar kWh are produced, showing that the technical growth margin — between permits, available roofs and ground-mounted systems — is there.
On the wind front, however, the recent acceleration of authorisation procedures and several projects in the pipeline could allow a partial recovery of the accumulated delay, notes SES. The reference is to federal simplifications aimed at unblocking processes that have been stalled for years, a hot political topic in Parliament and in the Alpine cantons.
### SES's requests to policymakers
"It is essential that politics guarantees framework conditions (for all green vectors) in the long term. Only in this way will it be possible to stimulate the necessary investments and durably carry forward the progress of the energy transition," SES writes in the press release accompanying the study. A request that closely concerns companies and investors called upon to plan plants with twenty-year horizons, and that weighs directly on the cost of energy for households and SMEs in the coming years.
For those who want to understand how much bills weigh on the family budget today, it is useful to compare the data on the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) and simulate the effect of electricity tariffs on the payslip with the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## What to do: the role of households, Cantons and investors
The 2025 SES study does not provide individual recipes, but it draws a clear perimeter within which households, Cantons and operators move. Here are the operational points that emerge from the data.
### For households
Taking advantage of the record photovoltaic figures is worthwhile, especially in a country where over 96% of new installations are rooftop-based. The balance between self-consumption and grid feed-in remains the key factor in reducing energy expenditure, an issue that directly affects the household [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living). In recent years the Confederation has introduced mechanisms for reimbursing the repurchase tariff, and several Cantons offer stackable cantonal incentives. Before installing a system, it is worth checking both the municipal regulations and the cantonal rates, because the difference in tax treatment between the energy component and excise duties varies from Canton to Canton.
### For Cantons and municipalities
The wind power figure (18 kWh per capita) and the recent acceleration of authorisation procedures indicate where the next few years will be decided. Alpine and pre-Alpine municipalities, in particular, remain the decisive hubs: without their technical and political green light, projects stay stuck. For local authorities, the challenge is intertwined with spatial planning, ecological compensation, and the share of taxes and water royalties linked to renewable production.
### For businesses and investors
Demand for solar and wind installations is clearly accelerating. According to SES, Swiss solar production increased by 2000 GWh in a single year, and the foundation's request is for stable, long-term framework conditions. For those considering an investment in the sector, three checks are essential: technical feasibility of the site, the cantonal and municipal authorisation process, and the subsidy or grid feed-in reimbursement regime.
### Scenario: what would change with more wind power

The Swiss National Bank has chosen the graphic design destined to become the tenth series of Swiss banknotes. The choice to tell Switzerland's story through altitude bands is not a stylistic exercise: it means crossing in six cuts the 4,850 metres that separate Lake Maggiore's water level from the 4,810 metres of the Dufourspitze, touching at least four of the six biogeographical regions recognised at federal level. It is an idea that enhances Swiss polycentrism, where the Confederation coexists with 26 cantons and roughly 2,100 municipalities, each with its own landscape identity. For an economy built on tourism, mountain agriculture, cutting-edge research and logistics infrastructure — from Alpine passes to freight rail corridors such as the Gotthardo — the narrative by altitudes translates into images what the macroeconomic figures from the FSO have been showing for years: the country's wealth is distributed across the entire vertical gradient, not only along the Zurich–Geneva–Basel axes.
### Practical implications for those who use the franc every day
For those who live and work in Switzerland the change will not hit wallets immediately: the ninth series will remain legal tender and no current banknote will be withdrawn in the coming years. What will change, gradually, is the user experience: cashiers, merchants and consumers will need to familiarise themselves with new graphic elements and, above all, with previously unseen security features — the most delicate chapter of any SNB issue, designed to resist counterfeiting.
An often overlooked aspect concerns machines: vending machines, parking meters, SBB ticket machines, turnstiles and ticket validators will need to be adapted to recognise the new banknotes. The application procedure for family allowances in Switzerland follows similar logic in all cantons, with cantonal adaptations regarding forms and the competent compensation fund. ### Step 1: identify the competent compensation fund
The first concrete step is to understand which fund to contact. For an employee, the fund is normally the employer's fund. ### Step 3: submit the application
The application is submitted to the competent family compensation fund. Once the allowance has been obtained, it is advisable to check the amount actually credited on the pay slip and compare it with what is provided for by Uri cantonal law. ## In a nutshell - Law on National Exhibitions: message approved on 26 August 2026 - No federal co-financing before 2040, confirmed by the Federal Council - Maximum federal contribution: 30% of eligible costs - Parliament may decide whether and when to co-finance, but not before 2035
## Key facts - **What**: Approval of the message on the new federal law on national exhibitions - When: 26 August 2026 - Where: Bern - Who: Federal Council - Mandate: CSEC-S Motion 23.3966, approved by Parliament in March 2024 - Time limit: Federal co-financing excluded before 2040 - Maximum federal share: 30% of eligible costs - Opinions collected in consultation: 52
### The decision of August 26, 2026 The Federal Council approved on 26 August 2026 the message regarding the new Federal Law on the Promotion of National Exhibitions. The text of the law lays the foundations for possible financial support by the Confederation for future national exhibitions, thus fulfilling the mandate of a motion approved by Parliament.
At the same time, the Executive confirmed its decision, taken in June 2025, not to co-finance such an exposure before 2040. The choice reflects the current spending priorities of the Confederation: in the coming years there are no resources to commit to a major event of this magnitude, even if the legal framework conditions are still defined.
### The role of ### What concretely changes for Cantons and Municipalities The new law redraws the perimeter of who can apply for federal funds for a national exposure and under what conditions. Before this message, the rules were not codified in a single text: each initiative was based on political decisions on a case-by-case basis. With the new federal law on the promotion of national exhibitions, the picture becomes explicit: no federal money without a concrete project, without a cantonal and municipal quota at least equivalent, and without a decision in principle of Parliament.
For a Canton wishing to apply to host a national exhibition, the message clarifies three operational aspects. First, the project must be sufficiently mature before applying for federal co-financing. Second: Cantons and Municipalities must guarantee at least 30% of the eligible costs, equal to the maximum federal share, so in fact the required co-financing ratio is one to one. Third: the Confederation does not issue deficit guarantees, exposing the promoters to the risk of covering any budget holes.
### The calendar that comes out of the message The roadmap set by the message is clear. The decision of parliamentary principle cannot be proposed before 2035. ## In a nutshell - Guy Parmelin visits a research company in Carrouge (Vaud) in solidarity with the agricultural world - Government suspends hay duties and reduces corn import tariffs: CHF 54 million aid - Fodder sorghum is a sustainable alternative to corn in drought situations

After Federal Councillor Albert Rösti yesterday, Confederation President Guy Parmelin today expressed solidarity with the Swiss agricultural world. Parmelin, head of the Federal Department of Economy, Training and Research (DEFR) and in this capacity responsible for the primary sector, visited a company in the Vodese countryside that experiments with potentially more drought-resistant crops.
The visit to Carrouge allowed the Minister of Agriculture — a former winegrower close to the farming world — to directly observe the experiments on fodder sorghum, a cereal native to Africa. Sabine Bach, head of the company, explained to reporters how sorghum needs relatively little water after sowing ## Federal support measures: suspension of duties and loans
The Swiss government has taken a number of concrete measures to support the agricultural sector during this summer crisis. The Confederation suspended customs duties on hay imports, immediately reducing supply costs for farmers who have to import fodder. In addition, customs tariffs for the import of maize intended for animal feed have been temporarily reduced, further facilitating access to livestock feed sources at lower prices.
In addition to these trade measures, Federal Councillor Albert Rösti, head of the Federal Department of the Environment (DETEC), announced aid of CHF 54 million for the current year. This amount is made available in the form of interest-free loans, specifically intended to support farms facing liquidity problems due to the shortage of fodder and extraordinary expenses for animal feed. This decision acknowledges that the drought has generated a temporary but severe cash crunch for many companies.

## In a nutshell - Center for unmanned systems with tech hub and military command from 2026 - Drone battalion operational since 2028 with its own recruit school - Investments in drone defense to protect critical infrastructure
## Key facts - **What**: Center for unmanned systems (tech hub + military command) - When: 27 August 2026 (announcement); operational battalion from 2028 - Where: Switzerland at federal level, in collaboration with cantons and private individuals - Who: DDPS (Federal Department of Defence, Population Protection and Sport) - References: Defence guidelines 19 June 2026; army message 2026; armament programme 2027
On 27 August 2026, the Federal Department of Defence, Population Protection and Sport (DDPS) announced a strategic breakthrough: drones, drone defence and robotics become national priorities to strengthen Switzerland's military capabilities.
The decision responds to a changed threat situation. Drones, powered by artificial intelligence, have radically transformed the way wars are conducted. In Switzerland, there is an increase in drone flights over military and critical infrastructure. At the same time, drones assert themselves as a tool of hybrid warfare, a mode of conflict that goes beyond the traditional military confrontation.
### Three pillars of the strategy
The DDPS structures the response on three main axes. First: the creation of a center for unmanned systems, ### How the drone systems center works
The new center integrates three crucial elements. The tech hub brings together the operational needs of the armed forces, the technological expertise of armasuisse (the federal armament agency), and knowledge from universities, startups and the private sector. The objective is to collaborate to develop, test and quickly deploy innovative solutions for military use.
The military command, on the other hand, manages an **organization for experimentation and training**: it tests new systems in realistic conditions and is responsible for training the drone battalion. A virtuous circle: the knowledge acquired by troops in the field is transmitted to the scientific and business world through the tech hub.
### Implications for the national defense system
The choice of shorter acquisition cycles and smaller quantities reflects the accelerated pace of technological innovation. The armed forces intend to acquire systems in a targeted manner, in short cycles, rapidly introducing what proves effective and developing it further based on acquired experience. This agile approach reduces the risks of technological obsolescence, a serious problem in the military sector due to the exponential progress of artificial intelligence and robotics.
For the system to function, seamless collaboration is required between institutional levels: federal, cantonal and private. The DDPS has provided that the center be accessible to other departments, cantons and emergency response organizations, expanding the public benefit of research and experimentation.
A parallel challenge concerns skills and legal bases in drone defense. Today this responsibility is fragmented among various public authorities and private infrastructure managers. An interdepartmental working group led by the DDPS is examining current competencies and evaluating necessary regulatory adjustments. Work is also proceeding following a parliamentary mandate (motion 25.4410), a sign of political interest in this critical issue.
### Opportunities for military careers and training
The establishment of a drone battalion and a dedicated recruit school opens new employment prospects within the Swiss armed forces. Personnel qualified in technology, robotics and artificial intelligence will have significant professional career opportunities. The DDPS also intends to benefit from the experience of militia personnel already active in the economic, scientific and technological sectors, creating bridges between the civil and Swiss military worlds. Investments will not stop in 2028. The military will continue the systematic integration of drone expertise throughout the military structure, adopting a continuous learning approach based on operational data and experiences acquired in the field.

Swiss cantons have a crucial role in defending against drone attacks, particularly those targeting critical regional infrastructure such as water and energy networks. ## In a nutshell - Vote on neutrality on September 27, 2026 - Kremlin uses RT.DE and social media to influence campaign - Federal Government Recognizes Growing Threat of Foreign Disinformation

The Kremlin has repeatedly tried to influence the campaign on Swiss neutrality in recent weeks, SRF reported. Swiss citizens will vote on the initiative on 27 September 2026. The proposal would write into the Swiss constitution a broad ban on sanctions against states involved in armed conflict, with the exception of Switzerland's obligations to the United Nations.
### Moscow's campaign through the media
RT.DE, a Kremlin-funded newspaper, published several articles during the campaign. These articles were critical of the Federal Council, which opposes the initiative, and supportive of the proposal. Some of these articles are attributed to Hans-Ueli Läppli, although no journalist by this name can be identified. The surname is familiar in Switzerland from Alfred Rasser's fictional character, Theophil Läppli, a Swiss soldier ## # Expert analysis and normalization strategy
Ulrich Schmid, professor of Eastern European studies at the University of St. Gallen, explained the significance of the Kremlin campaign to SRF. The Kremlin is trying to present the war in Ukraine as an ordinary two-state conflict. Adding neutrality to the Swiss constitution would play into the hands of the Kremlin, normalizing the conflict. Schmid predicts that such influence efforts will likely have little direct effect on Swiss voters' choices. However, he stresses that Switzerland should still take them seriously, as attempts to influence Swiss public opinion are part of a much broader Kremlin strategy of destabilization. This strategy is designed to operate in the long term, according to the scholar's analysis.
## # Federal Government Recognition and SEPOS Warning
The federal government recognizes the problem. In response to a request from SRF, the State Secretariat for Security Policy (SEPOS) stated that foreign disinformation and state-funded influence attempts, specifically targeting Switzerland, are on the rise. In a draft security policy document, SEPOS warns that foreign influence operations and disinformation can directly affect the results of elections and referendums. item.description: The Federal Council is asking for CHF 71.5 million to support forests and farmers affected by the record drought of 2026.

## In a nutshell - Government asks CHF 71.5 million for droughts and forests - CHF 17.5 million per year from 2027 for woodland adaptation - CHF 54 million in 2026 for cash-strapped farms - Record-low rainfall until mid-August 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Extraordinary federal funding for drought and agriculture - When: Discussion on Wednesday Federal Council; evaluation by the end of October, autumn decision - Where: Switzerland (Canton Zurich, Vaud, other affected regions) - Who: Federal Council; Parliament; DATEC, DEFR, DFI, DDPS - Amount: CHF 17.5 million forest credit 2027+ + CHF 54 million agriculture 2026 - Aid type: Interest-free receivables for liquidity - Sectors affected: Agriculture, forests, shipping, electricity
The Federal Council discussed on Wednesday the situation of heatwave and drought that is affecting Switzerland. The decision is clear: it calls on Parliament to allocate extraordinary funds to support farms and adapt forests to ongoing climate change.
The figures are significant. The executive calls for an increase of 17.5 million francs for forest credit in 2027. In addition, from 2028, the Federal Department of Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC) will be able to request funds of the same amount every year. For agriculture, the means rise by 54 million francs in 2026, as a one-off support for companies in liquidity crisis caused ### What Concretely Changes
The announced financing represents a break from the usual ordinary federal budget cycle. Normally, forest credit and agricultural aid follow standard and predictable paths of annual programming. This time, the Federal Council recognizes that the liquidity crisis for farmers is immediate and cannot wait for ordinary timelines. An emergency situation requires emergency tools.
The mechanism is simple from an operational standpoint: those who benefit are farmers affected by drought and public and private forest owners. How? Through bank credits guaranteed by the Confederation, interest-free. When? The 54 million for agriculture is already available in 2026; the 17.5 million for forests comes into force from 2027, with the possibility of annual renewal from 2028 onwards.
This means that a farm that has seen its harvests collapse, with emergency irrigation costs or livestock management costs drastically increased due to drought, can access these funds to maintain operational liquidity until the next production cycle. These are not direct aid (non-repayable subsidies), but subsidized financing that must be repaid. The absence of interest reduces the overall cost of the liquidity crisis.
### Implications for Affected Sectors
For agricultural enterprises, interest-free credit represents an essential injection of liquidity at a critical moment. The Confederation, through the cantons, supports agricultural enterprises to overcome the crisis without resorting to the ordinary credit market, where interest rates would be significantly higher and the availability of financing could be limited given the risk profile of the sector during periods of disaster.
For forests, the annual financing of 17.5 million (starting from 2027) allows cantons and owners to invest in concrete climate adaptation measures: emergency irrigation for young plants, selection and planting of drought-resistant forest species, prevention of wildfires through fuel reduction interventions. In Switzerland, forests are not purely private property: many belong to municipalities or cantons, and the public interest in keeping them healthy is evident from an economic and environmental perspective.
The subsequent expansion of annual appropriations (from 2028 the DATEC can request funds every year based on needs) suggests that the Government foresees a long-term situation, not an episodic one. The 2026 drought, with record-low precipitation until mid-August, may not be an isolated exception but a signal of structural climate change. For farmers, the 54 million francs allocated in 2026 are available through the ordinary channel of applying for concessional credit with cantonal administrations. Each canton has a specific office (usually the Department of Agriculture) responsible for managing these extraordinary funds. The agricultural enterprise in question must demonstrate concrete damage from drought — significantly reduced harvests, additional irrigation costs, livestock losses — and present a realistic financial repayment plan in order to access the credit.
The credit is interest-free, which means the enterprise repays only the principal borrowed, without any additional financial costs. This drastically reduces the cost of the crisis compared to an ordinary bank loan, where interest could absorb significant resources during the recovery period. The administrative procedure is streamlined compared to normal credit evaluation standards: there are no lengthy credit assessments, but rather a verification of the drought-related crisis situation.
For forest owners, the process is similar: the cantons make available 17.5 million annually (starting from 2027) through offices competent in forest management. The resources are intended for concrete adaptation projects — land reclamation, reforestation with resilient species, fire protection — which must be documented and authorized by the cantons before disbursement.
### What happens by October and autumn
The Government has set precise deadlines for following up on the situation. By the end of October, the federal departments DATEC, DEFR, DFI, and DDPS will complete a new in-depth analysis of the drought, energy, and agriculture situation. If the drought continues or other related crises emerge (for example, risks to hydroelectric energy production due to critical water levels in dams, river navigation problems, further agricultural losses), the Government could propose additional support measures.
In autumn (September–November 2026), the Federal Council will make a final decision on any new interventions that go beyond the already announced package of 71.5 million. This means that those awaiting a definitive response from the Government on additional measures should know that the most important decisions will come in the coming months of autumn 2026. In the meantime, cantonal administrations will be able to begin collecting applications and processing agricultural credit requests based on the 54 million allocated for 2026.
### Next operational steps
Those working in agriculture or owning forests in Switzerland should stay in contact with the competent cantonal office (Department of Agriculture or Forest) to understand how to access the funds and what the specific procedures are. The allocated amounts, application timelines, and conditions vary from canton to canton, although federal financing is coordinated at the central level by DATEC and departmental partners.

However, the picture becomes more complex when looking at total debt: gross public debt, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) definition, should increase in 2025 by approximately 5.4 billion francs.
The result is that Swiss gross public debt will reach 353.2 billion francs, equivalent to 40.7 percent of national gross domestic product. This means that for every 100 francs of wealth produced by the Swiss economy, public debt represents 40.7 francs — a measure of fiscal sustainability crucial for assessing the financial health of the country.
Data published by the Federal Finance Administration website includes three levels of detail: data from the 'Main Groups', 'Detailed SF Data' (financial statistics, with comparability at the national level) and 'Detailed GFS Data' (Government Finance Statistics, based on IMF international standards). An 'International Comparison' is also available to place Swiss budgets in a global context.
### What it means for taxpayers The public budget surplus is generally a positive sign for Swiss taxpayers, as it indicates that tax revenues — derived from federal direct tax, VAT, and cantonal and municipal taxes — exceed current spending. However, the simultaneous increase in gross public debt suggests that much of this wealth ends up in long-term financing mechanisms, often linked to public investments, welfare programs (AVS, LPP, LAMal benefits) and infrastructure.
Even if 2025 data shows an overall surplus, this does not necessarily mean that federal, cantonal, or municipal taxes will decrease. In the short term, the surplus could be allocated to pay off previous debts or to finance new social programs (AVS, LPP, LAMal). Anyone who resides or works in Switzerland should verify how this fiscal situation affects their [income tax return](nav:tax-return).
The volatility between annual surplus and debt accumulation illustrates how Swiss fiscal management follows long-term sustainability logic, not perfect annual balance. For this reason, taxpayers should not expect drastic fiscal decisions based on single budget years, but rather monitor the multi-year guidelines of the Federal Council and cantonal governments. Practical analysis: the coexistence of surplus and growing debt
The coexistence of a budget surplus and growing debt may seem contradictory, but it reflects a financial reality common to developed countries. Surplus represents the net balance between current receipts and outflows in a year, while gross debt is the stock accumulated over time by public liabilities — including loans, government debt securities, and future obligations towards welfare programs.
### Distribution of debt among levels of government Switzerland's 353.2 billion gross public debt is not concentrated at the federal level. The Federal Finance Administration provides a cross-analysis showing how the debt burden is distributed among the Confederation, Cantons and Municipalities. Each level of government has its own fiscal autonomy — each canton sets its own cantonal tax rates within federal limits, and each municipality sets its own municipal multiplier on a cantonal basis.

item.title: US duty reimbursement: administrative fear
item.description: Only a third of Swiss companies ask for reimbursement of improperly collected US duties. The others give up for fear of excessive administrative burdens.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Only 1/3 of Swiss companies request reimbursement of improperly collected US tariffs - They fear administrative costs exceeding financial gains - Online form available, but Swissmem should promote it better - Expected decline in overseas business activity for most companies
## Key facts - **What**: Reimbursement of US tariffs on machinery, electronics, metals sector - Who: Swissmem (Swiss industry association), Martin Hirzel (president) - Percentage of applicants: Only 1/3 of companies have requested reimbursement - Main obstacle: Fear of administrative costs vs. modest financial gain - Procedure: Online form available but 'rather complicated' - Communication: Swissmem does not adequately promote the procedure - Outlook: Majority of companies expect declining activity in the United States
Only one-third of Swiss companies active in the machinery, electronics, and metals sector have requested reimbursement from the United States for improperly collected tariffs. This was revealed by Martin Hirzel, president of the industry association Swissmem, in an interview with financial agency AWP. This data illuminates a significant discrepancy: two out of three companies formally forgo recovering amounts owed, despite the right being established and the procedure being technically accessible.
The reasons for this massive abstention are primarily administrative. Companies fear excessive bureaucratic costs in the face of modest financial gain. This creates a scenario in which the perceived cost of the request exceeds the expected benefit, discouraging action.
### The procedural transparency issue
Hirzel openly acknowledges that companies must fill out a 'rather complicated' form, although the procedure can be completed online. The paradox is evident: the digital channel exists, but the perception of complexity hinders participation. More significantly, the president does not exclude the association's own responsibility: 'Perhaps Swissmem should also promote this procedure more clearly', he stated.
This admission reveals a communication gap. If Swissmem could offer transparent guidance, support in document collection, and specific training on form completion, the participation rate would presumably increase. The gap between formal right and actual exercise is thus bridgeable, but requires active advocacy from the industry association.
In the broader context, companies have 'learned to coexist with customs tariffs', according to Hirzel. However, the distance from normalizing the commercial situation with the United States remains real. Tariff volatility and continual regulatory adjustments keep companies in a state of permanent adaptation. Those wishing to delve deeper into the tax implications of international business operations can consult [resources on tax returns and compliance](nav:tax-return). The administrative burden resulting from tariffs and constantly changing regulations exerts direct pressure on the profitability and operational capacity of companies. Companies do not only face the immediate economic problem of tariffs, but also the hidden costs associated with compliance, management of international documentation, and continuous updating of internal processes.
A concrete consequence is the uncertainty transmitted to international customers. American buyers of Swiss products in the machinery, electronic components, and metal goods sectors operate in a precarious situation. Profit margins remain uncertain, delivery times undergo variations due to administrative obstacles, final prices remain exposed to tariff volatility. This creates a spiral of risks that discourages volume orders and long-term contracts.
### Predictions of Contraction and Communication Failure
The majority of interviewed Swissmem companies predict a decline in overseas activity. This is not a marginal forecast: the American market remains strategic for the Swiss precision industry. A widespread contraction in exports to the USA would entail cascading repercussions on employment, research and development investments, and overall sector competitiveness.
The problem of inadequate communication emerges clearly from Hirzel's statement. If the reimbursement procedure remains poorly known and underutilized, the economic loss for companies accumulates over time, year after year. This is not a single recovery, but a series of missed reimbursements that progressively erode operating margins and investment capacity.
Constantly changing regulations further amplify the damage. Every change in customs rules or tariff rates entails the need for internal updates, staff training, and process revision. For small and medium-sized companies, these administrative costs can be significant and difficult to absorb, especially if they simultaneously lose market share due to tariff instability. Companies thus find themselves trapped in a cycle of increasing administrative costs facing increasingly uncertain revenues.
For those operating in the international commercial field and needing to understand currency dynamics in real time, [the CHF/EUR exchange rate comparator provides current data](nav:exchange).

Companies interested in recovering duties improperly collected have access to a formal procedure with the American customs authorities. Although the form is complex, online filing remains the only effective way to recover the amounts owed and should not discourage initiative. The first operational step is to contact the American customs authorities (U.S. Customs and Border Protection) directly, or to contact Swissmem to obtain initial informational support on the procedure and required documentation.
The procedure requires: precise identification of duties paid in excess; collection of commercial documentation (invoices, licenses, certificates of origin, original customs declarations); accurate completion of the specific form according to American criteria. Although the process can be completed online, it is essential to devote sufficient time to collecting documentation and verifying data accuracy. Procedural errors result in rejection of the request and loss of the right to reimbursement.
### How to proceed effectively
Swissmem could develop a crucial role in providing technical assistance to members: step-by-step guides, training webinars on completion, referrals to customs tariff experts, standardized document templates. Currently, President Hirzel has explicitly acknowledged that this support function is insufficient. Companies proceeding independently must nevertheless evaluate the cost-benefit: if the expected reimbursement is less than CHF 5,000–10,000 (not specified in the source, but realistic for average amounts), spending on external consulting could erode the entire net gain.
A strategic element is timing. Duty recovery is not immediate and requires administrative patience and following specific procedures. Interested companies must proceed without delay, as there are presumably time limits for claims under American regulations (although not explicitly stated in Hirzel's communication).
Furthermore, exporting companies should comprehensively evaluate their commercial strategy towards the USA in a strategic perspective. If customs regulations remain unstable and administrative costs high, geographic diversification of markets, reconsideration of price margins, or negotiation of contracts with tariff adjustment clauses could prove strategic. For those managing small and medium-sized enterprises and wishing to evaluate the economic impact of commercial decisions on the Swiss corporate structure and financial planning, [the salary and tax calculator offers a basis for modeling scenarios](nav:calculator).

## In brief - Federal Council allocates CHF 73 million to address drought and summer heat - CHF 54 million for farmers, CHF 17.5 million for forests until 2031 - Roundtable by end of October to identify additional support measures
## Key facts - **What**: Federal allocation of CHF 73 million to mitigate effects of summer 2026 drought - When: Announced on August 27, 2026 during federal press conference - Where: Federal level (Federal Council, DATEC) - Who: Albert Rösti (federal councillor), Lisa Mazzone (Greens president), Jürg Grossen (Green Liberals president) - Amount: CHF 73 million total (CHF 54 M agriculture + CHF 17.5 M forests) - Period: Forest funds guaranteed until 2031
The Federal Council is allocating 73 million francs to mitigate the effects of summer drought. This is announced by federal councillor Albert Rösti, head of the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DATEC), during a press conference in which he responds to criticism over alleged slowness in responding to the heat wave.
In the package of measures, the Government allocates 54 million francs to farmers, as compensation for loss of income caused by drought. An additional credit of 17.5 million finances forests until 2031, reintroducing funds previously cut in the federal savings package. For the rest, the Confederation has tasked a roundtable with offices and experts to identify additional needs by the end of October and propose any further measures.
Rösti defends the Federal Council's climate policy as a result of political compromises. The Confederation, he emphasizes, already spends 115 million francs per year on forests. To which are added the 17.5 million announced today, a figure set to double with cantonal contributions. These funds are not limited to 2027, but guaranteed until 2031. More broadly, the Confederation invests approximately 3 billion francs in global climate measures: climate protection, decarbonization, abandonment of fossil fuels, protection of biodiversity and adaptation to climate change.
The political reaction is divided. Lisa Mazzone, president of the Greens, criticizes Rösti's actions bluntly: 'There isn't much in practice. Help for agriculture, very good. But for the rest, it doesn't get to the root of the problem: no measures for cities, health, the population... nothing'. Different is the position of the Green Liberals: their president Jürg Grossen states: 'What is being proposed today is insufficient, the response is also too slow, but it is something. We will support these measures'.
The Swiss Farmers' Union and BoscoSvizzero, the association of forest owners, welcome the assistance positively. He also emphasizes that it is important to maintain the right proportions by looking at what happens in other parts of the world: we must slow climate change with protective measures, abandon fossil fuels and adapt.
